A1.justification: Both PDFs describe StreamAvatar with the same authors and core framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, interactive-generation evaluations, a 24-participant user study, and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds long-video examples and runtime sensitivity measurements.

M1.justification: The two-stage distillation/refinement framework, Reference Sink, RAPR, consistency-aware discriminator, and talking/listening conditioning remain the same. The added teacher-training, audio-alignment, and deployment descriptions disclose implementation details without establishing a change to the earlier procedure.

E1.justification: Training still uses SpeakerVid-5M and self-collected videos; evaluation retains the short/long avatar sets, EMTD, and SpeakerVid-5M interactive samples. The longer rollouts extend the existing long-video task without introducing a distinct dataset, domain, or interaction scenario.

E2.justification: The talking baselines and OmniAvatar-based interactive baseline are unchanged. INFP, ARIG, MIDAS, and X-Streamer already appear in v1's appendix comparisons. Table 4's discriminator-ablation row is renamed from +GAN w/o global to +GAN w/o DCA, retaining its results.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported RAPR distance from D=10 to D=9, without establishing that experiments were rerun. Added evaluations vary chunk size C=1,3,5 and KV-cache length, and show rollouts up to 150 seconds. Existing benchmark sample counts and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds focused supplementary checks: long-duration stability examples in Section 7.6/Figure 11 and chunk-size/cache-length runtime sensitivity in Section 8/Figure 12. It also reports that replacing future audio features has negligible quality impact. Existing component and audio-mask ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The user study remains 24 participants and 960 paired comparisons; converting its chart to a table does not change statistical reporting practices.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 4 retain their numerical entries but reverse IQA/ASE attribution: Table 1's short-set Ours scores change from IQA=3.03, ASE=4.68 to IQA=4.68, ASE=3.03. v2 adds long-video stability examples and runtime curves showing latency/throughput tradeoffs. Other benchmark values and user-study preferences are retained; these changes do not establish a performance gain.

T1.justification: Section 3.1.1 corrects the chunk-end definition from e_i=s_i*C to e_i=i*C, fixing the stated block boundaries. Appendix Equation (1) explicitly defines audio-to-latent temporal alignment. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and main technical contributions remain unchanged. The conclusion relaxes the speed claim from orders of magnitude faster to significantly faster, removing the stronger magnitude assertion while retaining the claimed efficiency advantage.

C2.justification: The limitations now acknowledge motion-range constraints from distillation and limited semantic control from simplistic text handling. Section 8 adds explanations of latency, throughput, and temporal-context tradeoffs. The RAPR discussion also replaces guaranteeing stability with improving stability.

D1.justification: New Appendix Section 6 substantially expands reproducibility information: VAE compression, reference-latent conditioning, audio context windows and projectors, frame-wise attention, the flow-matching objective, and freeze/unfreeze teacher training. Section 8 additionally explains deployed audio-lookahead handling and chunk-buffer latency. These are substantial disclosures about the existing implementation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including TalkingGaussian, StyleTalk, Flow Matching, and Rectified Flow, and expands the discussion of MIDAS and X-Streamer. Section 4.1 narrows the earlier assertion that unified full-body interactive methods had not been achieved to the absence of an open-source comparator, acknowledging the closed-source methods already compared in v1.

P1.justification: v2 edits grammar and terminology, rewrites selected introduction and related-work passages, moves qualitative ablation explanations into the main text, and reorganizes the appendix around the added teacher details. The overall narrative and main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: Several displays receive substantial revisions: Figure 4 is rebuilt as a fuller architecture diagram, Figure 3 is reformatted and moved, and the user-study chart becomes Table 5. New Figures 11–12 present long-video examples and runtime sensitivity, while existing qualitative panels are resized and rearranged. Tables 1 and 4 also change metric headers.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reproducibility through explicit teacher-training and audio-processing details, adds useful evidence about long-duration generation and runtime tradeoffs, and states more informative limitations. Clearer displays and the corrected chunk definition also help. The overall gain is limited: core comparative evidence is retained, long-duration validation remains qualitative, and the revised RAPR setting is not accompanied by an explanation of whether results were rerun.
